paper_identity: The PDF is Jurić-Lekić G, Bedrica Lj, Lončar D (2018) "Interscapular brown adipose tissue recruitment is hindered by a temperature environment of 33°C: uncoupling protein-1 underexpression is not associated with obesity development in rats." Arch Biol Sci 70(3):567-579 (doi 10.2298/ABS171215018J). This matches the sheet metadata: author "Juric-Lekic", year 2018, Mammalia / Rattus norvegicus / Sprague-Dawley rat, brown adipose tissue. The sheet citation string "Juric_Kekic_et_al_2018" is a misspelling of Jurić-Lekić but clearly the same paper. Tissue in the sheet (brown adipose tissue, IBAT) is correct.
error_statistic_reported: SD. Table 2 title reads "morphological parameters (±SD)" and its footnote states "Data are the mean±SD from three animals in each group" (p. 572). Table 3 footnote: "Data are the mean±SD from three animals in each group" (p. 574). Table 4 footnote: same (p. 576). Table 1: "The mean (±SD) represents the measurements of ten randomly selected animals" (p. 571). The sheet correctly places the tabulated ± values in sd_t1/sd_t2 and derives se = sd/sqrt(3) (e.g. merged_422: sd_t1 12 -> se_t1 6.928; sd_t2 17 -> se_t2 9.815). No SEM-as-SD problem anywhere in this study.
stated_sample_sizes: n = 3 per group per age for every extracted row. Methods p. 569: "The experimental and control groups of animals were killed simultaneously at 7, 14 and 30 days of age. Six young animals from each age group were killed: 3 for morphology/electron microscopy studies and 3 for mRNA essays." Table 2 and Table 3 headers both read "20°C (n-3)" / "33°C (n-3)" (typographic "n-3" for n=3) with footnotes confirming three animals per group. The morphometry rested on 4 IBAT samples per animal x 100 EM images, but the biological n is 3 — correctly used. Sheet n_t1 = n_t2 = 3 for all 15 rows: correct. (Table 1 whole-animal data, n=10, was not extracted — appropriately, as it is not a mitochondrial measure.)
temperature_treatments: Two levels only: 33°C (experimental/thermoneutral) vs 20°C (room temperature control). Methods p. 569: "six pregnant Sprague-Dawley rats were placed in a temperature environment of 33°C, and six pregnant animals were kept at room temperature (20°C)"; the paper repeatedly calls the 20°C animals "the control group". The sheet assigns t1 = 33 (treatment) and t2 = 20 (control), with mean_t1/sd_t1 taken from the 33°C column and mean_t2/sd_t2 from the 20°C column in every row — correct, including the correct control identification. dose = 13 (the 13°C offset) is consistent.
multiple_stressors: No second manipulation. Temperature is the only experimental factor: both groups had a 12-h light-dark cycle, unlimited standard chow and tap water, individual caging of dams, and all litters culled to 9 pups (p. 569), so litter size and nutrition were equalised rather than crossed. No UV, hypoxia, diet, CORT, salinity or acute assay-temperature factor exists; measurements are EM morphometry, slot-blot mRNA and immuno-EM on fixed tissue, so there is no acute assay temperature to worry about. Every sheet row therefore comes from the baseline level of all other factors. No drug/supplement treatment, no cell culture, and the 20°C control is an experimentally assigned group, not field/seasonal acclimatisation.
developmental_timing: All animals were well before sexual maturity: pups were killed at 7, 14 and 30 days of age (p. 569), weaned at day 20; Sprague-Dawley sexual maturity is ~6 weeks, so the treatment does not span into sexual maturity. However, the stage/duration coding in the sheet is wrong (see finding 2). The sheet codes stage = "prenatal" with prenatal_trt_start = 17, prenatal_trt_end = 22, prenatal_dur = 5 days, total_trt_duration = 5 days, all postnatal treatment fields blank, and postnatal_measure_delay = 7/14/30 days. In fact the exposure was continuous prenatal AND postnatal: dams were moved to 33°C on gestation day 17 and "their pups were delivered and raised at 33°C" for the whole first month (Abstract; Methods p. 569; Results p. 570), so animals were still in their assigned thermal environment at the moment of sacrifice. Correct coding: prenatal ~5 d (GD17-birth) plus postnatal 0-7, 0-14 and 0-30 d; total duration ~12, ~19 and ~35 d; measurement delay = 0 for all rows.

This matches the sheet metadata exactly: author "Schnell", year 2008, class Actinopterygii, genus/species Oreochromis mossambicus, common name Tilapia. No identity problem.
error_statistic_reported: SEM. Statistical Analysis section, p. 736: "All data are presented as mean +/- 1 SE." Every figure caption repeats this: Fig. 1 "mean +/- SEM", Fig. 2 "means +/- SEM", Fig. 3 "n = 15; mean +/- SEM", Fig. 4 "mean +/- SEM". Also Animal Husbandry, p. 734: mass "8.99 +/- 1.12 g (mean +/- SE)". The sheet handles this correctly: the digitised bar half-width is stored in se_t1/se_t2 and sd_t1/sd_t2 = se * sqrt(15) for all 28 cells (verified numerically - sd/se = 3.8730 = sqrt(15) in every cell, implied n = 15.00). No un-converted-SEM problem in this study.
stated_sample_sizes:
Stated: 108 juveniles collected; randomly allocated to three acclimation groups of n = 36, each comprising three replicate tanks of n = 12 (p. 734). Within each treatment, 5 fish per tank (n = 5 x 3 = 15) were used for swimming/whole-animal MO2, and "a different five fish per replicate tank (n = 5 x 3 = 15 fish per acclimation treatment)" were used for mitochondrial MO2 and enzyme activities (p. 734). Fig. 3 caption explicitly states n = 15; Fig. 4 gives no n.

The sheet uses n_t1 = n_t2 = 15 for all 14 rows. This matches the Methods statement. However, the reported ANOVA degrees of freedom are only partly consistent with it:
- Mitochondrial MO2 (Fig. 3): F2,40 and F4,160 (state 3/state 4), F2,41 and F4,164 (RCR) -> 43-44 animals total, i.e. ~14-15 per group. Consistent with n = 15; the sheet's n is fine for merged_437-442.
- Enzyme activities (Fig. 4): every test is F2,24 (acclimation) and F4,96 (temperature) -> N - 3 = 24, so only 27 animals total, i.e. 9 per group. This contradicts n = 15 for the eight enzyme rows (merged_443-450). Reported as a finding.
temperature_treatments: Three acclimation temperatures, held for 28 d: 14.1 +/- 0.06, 17.2 +/- 0.03 and 22.2 +/- 0.04 degC (p. 734). The paper states 22 degC "represents water temperature at the collection site, which is also the current southernmost (coolest) limit of the fish", and all fish were held at 22.0 +/- 1.5 degC for 14 d before allocation. 22 degC is therefore unambiguously the correct control/reference, and the sheet's assignment (t2 = 22 in all 14 rows; t1 = 14 or 17) is right. dose (t1 - t2) = -8 and -5 is correct. Ramping was 2 degC/d and those days were excluded from the 28 d, correctly reflected in total_trt_duration = 28 days.
multiple_stressors:
Yes - the design crosses acclimation temperature with ACUTE TEST TEMPERATURE as a within-subject repeated measure: every mitochondrial and enzyme assay was run at 12, 14, 17, 22 and 26 degC (Methods pp. 734-735; Statistical Analysis p. 736: "Experimental temperatures (12, 14, 17, 22, and 26 degC) were treated as repeated measures"). There is no other manipulation - no UV, hypoxia, diet, CORT, drug or salinity treatment - so criterion 3 is satisfied and the study is admissible.

All 14 sheet rows were digitised from the 22 degC acute-test-temperature column of each panel, which I verified panel by panel. This is the defensible baseline choice and matches the extractor note ("we are only including data from 22C assay temperature as this is the temperature of the control group"): 22 degC is both the holding temperature and the control group's acclimation temperature, so the control cell is at its own thermal baseline. No rows come from a non-baseline level of the second factor. Worth recording as a moderator/caveat only: because a common 22 degC assay temperature was used, the 14 and 17 degC groups are measured 5-8 degC above their acclimation temperature, so these effect sizes are "common-garden" contrasts rather than each-at-its-own-temperature contrasts. Not flagged as a defect.

Non-independence is heavy and correctly annotated: all 7 measures come from the same 15 fish per group, and the same animals contribute the other four acute test temperatures (not extracted). RCR is additionally the arithmetic ratio of the state 3 and state 4 rows, so merged_437-442 are three non-independent effect sizes on one set of animals. The sheet's sample_depend column handles this.
developmental_timing: Correct. Animals were juvenile Oreochromis mossambicus, and the paper states explicitly on p. 734: "Fish were sexually immature, so sex was not included as a factor in the experimental design." Treatment therefore ran entirely pre-sexual-maturity and did not span into maturity, so criterion 1 is met and criterion 3's "treatments spanning development into sexual maturity" exclusion does not apply. The coding stage = postnatal is right (free-living juvenile fish, no prenatal exposure), and the prenatal_* fields are correctly left empty. Ages are not given in the paper; the extractor's estimate (postnatal_trt_start = 66.5 d, from a median sexual-maturity age of ~105 d) is a documented, reasonable imputation, but the start/end/duration fields do not reconcile with each other and the measure-delay field is mis-sourced - both reported as low-severity findings. sex = "both" is a defensible placeholder given the paper could not sex the fish.

Autoflags: all 7 were [SHARED CONTROL] flags. All 7 are FALSE ALARMS in the sense that they are correct and already properly annotated. The design genuinely has one 22 degC group (n = 36 allocated, 15 sampled for tissues) that is legitimately re-compared against both the 14 degC and the 17 degC groups, and the sheet encodes this with sample_depend = 1 (14 vs 22) / 2 (17 vs 22) and control_multiple_comparisons = "yes". A second, deeper layer of dependence is also correctly encoded: Methods (p. 735, "Enzyme Activities") state "Enzyme activities were measured in tissue samples taken from the same individuals used for mitochondrial respiration", so all 7 measures (muscle state 3/state 4/RCR/CCO/LDH and liver CCO/LDH) come from the same 15 fish per group - the shared sample_depend value across all rows of a contrast captures this. No shared-control finding raised.

paper_identity: PDF is Sant'Anna, G.M. & Mortola, J.P. (2003) "Thermal and respiratory control in young rats exposed to cold during postnatal development", Comparative Biochemistry and Physiology Part A 134: 449-459 (received 5 Aug 2002, accepted 29 Oct 2002). Species: pathogen-free male Sprague-Dawley rats (Rattus norvegicus), Mammalia. This matches the sheet's study metadata (year 2003, Rattus norvegicus, Sprague Dawley, class Mammalia); the sheet's `author` field is garbled as "San't Anne" (should be Sant'Anna), which is cosmetic only. Note the same folder contains the companion paper "Sant'Anna & Mortola 2002_Noble6" (the caloric-restriction/growth study) - a different paper, so there is no duplicate-data risk between N5 and N6 for this row.
error_statistic_reported: SEM. Methods section 2.5 ("Number of animals, and statistical analysis", p. 452): "We used five litters per group, each litter with six animals. Then, measurements were performed on four animals/litter, chosen randomly among the six, for a total of N=20 per group. All data are reported as means +/- 1 S.E.M." The Table 1 footnote repeats it: "Values are group means +/- 1 S.E.M. Number of animals was 20 in each group." The sheet correctly puts 8 and 6 in se_t1/se_t2 (the values printed in Table 1) and does not leave sd == se, so the SEM was recognised and converted; the only issue is the n used in the conversion (see findings).
stated_sample_sizes: Paper states N = 20 per group for Table 1 (Methods 2.5 and Table 1 footnote), arising from 5 litters/group x 4 of 6 pups measured. The sheet uses n_t1 = n_t2 = 5, i.e. litters, deliberately: the extractor note says "Sample size is five independent litters, even though say n = 20 / treatment. Avoid pseudoreplication use a conservative sample size". The pseudoreplication concern is legitimate (the unit of temperature assignment was the litter - "At day 1, the litter was assigned to one of two groups"), but the paper's printed SEM is an N=20 SEM, so pairing it with n=5 via sd = se*sqrt(5) is internally inconsistent (finding 2).
temperature_treatments: Two groups, assigned at the litter level on postnatal day 1 (Methods, p. 452): Control litters "continued to grow at the same ambient conditions", i.e. the colony/dam temperature of Ta ~23 degrees C; Cold litters "were raised at 14 degrees C from day 1 to 21" (in a fridge with the door ajar, Ta held steadily at 14 degrees C by thermocouple). So the biologically appropriate control/reference is 23 degrees C and the treatment is 14 degrees C (cold). The sheet has this backwards: t1 (treatment slot) = 23 with mean_t1 = 100 (the Control column of Table 1) and t2 (control slot) = 14 with mean_t2 = 161 (the Cold column). `dose` = 9 degrees C is the correct magnitude of the differential either way. The reversal is not a sheet-wide convention: across the other 40 study files t2 is consistently the repeated reference value (e.g. '22' in N17, '20' in s29, '28' in s44, '37' in Stier s2/s33, and literally 'control' in s59), so N5 is the odd one out.
multiple_stressors: No second developmental manipulation - developmental temperature (14 vs 23 degrees C, days 1-21) is the only factor, both groups had free access to food and water, and no drugs or supplements were given during the treatment window. The study does apply ACUTE challenges at the time of measurement (days 30-34): acute ambient temperatures of 5, 15, 25 and 35 degrees C, acute hypoxia (10% O2) and acute hypercapnia (5% CO2), plus halothane anaesthesia for telemetry implantation and terminal barbiturate. These are measurement conditions applied identically to both groups, not crossed developmental treatments, and the extracted UCP row comes from terminal tissue sampling after all of them ("On termination of the physiological measurements..."), so it is not drawn from a non-baseline level of a second factor. The acute-Ta and gas rows (Fig. 2, Tables 2-3) were correctly not extracted.
developmental_timing: Correct and unambiguous. Cold exposure ran postnatal day 1 to 21 in male Sprague-Dawley rats; tissue was collected at postnatal days 30-34 (Table 1 gives age 33 +/- 0.5 and 33 +/- 0.1 days). Male rats reach sexual maturity at roughly 6-7 weeks, so the entire treatment and the measurement precede sexual maturity - inclusion criteria 1 and 3 are satisfied. Sheet coding is right: stage = postnatal, postnatal_trt_start = 1, postnatal_trt_end = 21, dur_trt_postnatal = 20 days, total = 20 days, prenatal fields blank (the dam was housed at ~23 degrees C throughout pregnancy, so there was no prenatal thermal manipulation). postnatal_measure_delay = 11 days is consistent with sampling at day 30-34 after treatment ended on day 21 (true range 9-13 days). Shared controls are not an issue: this is a single row, sample_depend = 1 and control_multiple_comparisons = "no" are appropriate.
coverage: Only one row exists (merged_421) and I traced it to a specific line of a specific table. Sheet `ref` = "table1"; Table 1 ("Hematocrit, lung and BAT", p. 454) lists two UCP lines: "UCP/actin (% of Control): 100 +/- 16 vs 153 +/- 10, P<0.01" and "UCP/wet tissue (% of Control): 100 +/- 8 vs 161 +/- 6, P<0.001". The sheet's values (100 +/- 8 se; 161 +/- 6 se) and its `units` string "protein/wet mass (% of control)" unambiguously identify the UCP/wet-tissue line, so the correct row of the table was taken, measure identity (UCP, Western blot, Methods 2.4 p. 452, citing Mortola & Naso 1997) is right, tissue is right (interscapular brown adipose tissue; sheet tissue = "brown adipose tissue", tissue_sum = "adipose"), and mito_efficiency_dir = 0 is right for uncoupling protein. The UCP/actin line and BAT total protein (69.1 vs 114.0 mg/g) were not extracted - appropriate, since extracting UCP/actin as well would double-count the same measure. No physiological rows (VO2, ventilation, Tb, lung DNA/protein) belong in a mitochondrial-function sheet. Automated flags: none were raised for N5, so nothing to confirm or dismiss. The four problems I do report are: reversed t1/t2 group assignment, the SD-from-SEM/n scaling, sex coded "both" for an all-male study, and an arguable measurement_category.

paper_identity: The PDF is Li S, Li J, Chen W, Xu Z, Xie L, Zhang Y (2021) "Effects of Simulated Heat Wave on Oxidative Physiology and Immunity in Asian Yellow Pond Turtle (Mauremys mutica)", Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 9:704105, doi 10.3389/fevo.2021.704105 (11 pp.). This matches the sheet metadata exactly: citation Li_et_al_2021, author Li, year 2021, class Reptilia, genus Mauremys, species mutica, common name "Asian yellow pond turtle".
error_statistic_reported: SEM. Statistical Analysis, p. 4: "Data are expressed as the mean +/- SE." Every figure caption repeats it: Figure 1 (p. 4), Figure 2 (p. 5), Figure 3 (p. 5), Figure 4 (p. 6) and Figure 5 (p. 6) all read "Data were represented as mean +/- standard error (SE)". No SDs, CIs or ranges are reported anywhere; Table 2 (p. 4) gives only F/H and P values. The sheet handles this correctly in principle - all 20 group entries satisfy sd = se x sqrt(10) exactly, and 18 of the 20 se values match the error bar I measured in the figure. The two exceptions are the findings above: merged_389 se_t2 (sheet 0.193 vs plotted ~0.62, so its sd is really the plotted SEM) and merged_388 se_t1 (sheet 0.0030 vs plotted ~0.19).
stated_sample_sizes: n = 10 per group. Experimental Procedure, p. 3: 30 yearling turtles total; "ten randomly selected turtles were left in the incubator and defined as the 'control group' (n = 10)"; "randomly selected ten turtles which had been exposed to heat waves (heat wave group, n = 10)"; "recovery group, n = 10". Table 2 (p. 4) reports F(2,27) for TAC, CAT and SOD in both tissues and for muscle MDA/GSH, consistent with 30 animals in 3 groups. The sheet's n_t1 = n_t2 = 10 on all 10 rows is correct. (The only smaller n in the paper is the HSP qPCR, 4 individuals per group, F(2,9), Fig 5 - no HSP rows were extracted, so this does not affect the sheet.)
temperature_treatments: Three thermal groups (p. 3): (1) control, held at a fluctuating 28 +/- 4 C ten-step daily ramp for the 1-week experimental period - this is the acclimation regime and the stated set-point range of M. mutica (25-29 C), so it is the biologically appropriate reference; (2) heat wave, a fluctuating 35 +/- 4 C ramp for 1 week (peaks of 37-39 C for ~5 h/day, ~2 C below the species' CTmax of ~41 C); (3) recovery, 1 week heat wave then 1 week back at 28 +/- 4 C. The sheet assigns the heat-wave group to t1 (treatment) and the 28 C control to t2 (reference), which is the correct orientation, and every mean I checked is from the heat-wave bar rather than the recovery bar. The recovery group was correctly excluded (its animals had a second, sequential thermal manipulation and a 10-day delay). The only problem is the numeric value of t1: coded 34 C rather than the stated 35 C, with dose 6 rather than 7 (see findings).
multiple_stressors: No. Temperature is the only manipulated factor; it is not crossed with UV, hypoxia, diet, CORT, salinity or an acute assay temperature. All turtles were housed identically (individual boxes, 5 cm water, 13L:11D, the same commercial diet fed daily at 10:00, daily water changes) and received no drugs or supplements (pp. 2-3). Assays were run with standard commercial kits at fixed wavelengths, so there is no acute test-temperature factor. The only other level of any second factor is the sequential recovery period, and the extractor explicitly excluded that group - so all 10 sheet rows come from the baseline design (heat wave vs control, sampled immediately after the 1-week exposure). Note that the 10 rows do share a single control group: the same 10 control turtles supply mean_t2 for all five assays in both tissues, and the same 10 heat-wave turtles supply mean_t1. sample_depend = 1 captures this; control_multiple_comparisons = "no" is also right, because only one treatment arm was extracted, so the control is not re-used across multiple treatment levels.
developmental_timing: Yes, animals were well before sexual maturity. The subjects were "30 yearling M. mutica (carapace length 53.0 +/- 0.6 mm; body weight 30.4 +/- 1.1 g)" purchased from a farm in late July 2018 (p. 3) - juveniles far below maturity size for this species. The manipulation was entirely post-hatching, so stage = "postnatal" is correct and leaving all prenatal fields (prenatal_trt_start/end/dur/unit, prenatal_measure_delay) blank is correct. Duration coding is right: 1 week of heat wave (dur_trt_postnatal = 7 days, total 7 days), and postnatal_measure_delay = 0 days matches sampling between 07:00 and 09:00 immediately at the end of the exposure week. One caveat I judged not worth a finding: the paper never states an age, only "yearling", and the sheet encodes postnatal_trt_start = 546 d / end = 553 d (an assumed 1.5 years, disclosed in the extractor note). A yearling bought in late July, from a species hatching the previous late summer/autumn, is closer to 330-380 days old, and treatment actually began after a further 1-week acclimation. Either figure leaves the animals pre-maturity, so the stage classification and inclusion are unaffected. Separately, a scope judgement for the review team rather than an extraction error: this is an acute 1-week heat wave applied to a ~1-year-old juvenile and framed by the authors as acute heat stress, not a developmental-plasticity design; it satisfies inclusion criterion 1 as written (temperature manipulated experimentally before sexual maturity), but it sits at the "acute stress in a juvenile" end of that definition.
coverage: All 10 rows were traced to a specific panel. Figure 1 (p. 4, MDA) -> merged_381 (liver) and merged_386 (muscle); Figure 2A (p. 5, TAC) -> merged_382/merged_387; Figure 2B (CAT) -> merged_383/merged_388; Figure 2C (GSH-Px) -> merged_384/merged_389; Figure 2D (SOD) -> merged_385/merged_390. Means and error bars were re-measured by pixel-analysing 400-dpi renders of pp. 4-5 against each panel's y-axis tick calibration (Fig 1: 393 px/unit; Fig 2A: 316 px/unit; 2B: 15.82 px/unit; 2C: 21.08 px/unit; 2D: 0.903 px/unit). Agreement with the sheet was good everywhere (liver GSH-Px control measured 12.65 +/- 2.04 vs sheet 12.82 +/- 2.015; liver TAC heat wave 1.399 +/- 0.228 vs sheet 1.406 +/- 0.238, etc.). The sheet handles this correctly. For all 31 rows the se_* column holds the published/digitised SEM and sd_* = se_* x sqrt(8); I checked all 62 group entries programmatically and every one satisfies sd = se*sqrt(n) to within 2% (e.g. kris_n_521: se_t1 0.44 -> sd_t1 1.2445 = 0.44 x 2.8284). temperature_treatments:
Two developmental temperatures. Both treatments started in constant-temperature rooms at 20 degC; at the start of the experiment the cold-acclimated group's room was brought "down to 10 degC over 6 h", while "The other constant temperature room remained at 20 degC throughout the experiment, and is considered control because there was no change from the environmental temperature where the tadpoles were captured" (Methods 2.1, p. 733). Field water temperature at capture was 20 degC, so 20 degC is unambiguously the biologically appropriate reference.

The sheet's coding of t1 = 10 (treatment) and t2 = 20 (control), dose = -10 celsius, is therefore correct on all 31 rows, and the values are placed in the right columns for the 22 Table 1 rows (CS and CCO, verified digit-for-digit against the "Control" and "Cold-acclimated" rows) and for the two liver rows. Temperature is crossed with exactly one other factor: ASSAY (measurement) temperature. Every individual's tissue was assayed at 10, 20 and 30 degC ("Assays of tissue from each individual were completed at 10, 20 and 30 degC", p. 733) and the analyses treat assay temperature as a factor ("The effect of time of sampling, assay temperature (10, 20 or 30 degC), and treatment ... was analysed by a three-factor ANOVA", p. 734).

All 31 sheet rows come from the baseline level of that second factor, i.e. the 20 degC assay temperature, which is also the control rearing temperature:
- Axial muscle CS/CCO (kris_n_521-542): Table 1 reports only the 20 degC assay ("at assay temperature of 20 degC", caption p. 735) - no choice was involved.
- Axial muscle LDH (kris_n_514-520): Fig. 2 caption states "at 20 degC".
- Liver LDH and CS (kris_n_543, kris_n_544): Fig. 3 plots all three assay temperatures; I pixel-verified that the extracted numbers are the 20 degC bar pair in each panel (LDH 39.67/7.98 vs sheet 40.29/9.02; CS 8.85/6.70 vs sheet 8.756/6.631), not the 10 or 30 degC bars.

So no sheet row is drawn from a non-baseline level of the second factor. No other manipulations exist: no UV, hypoxia, diet, CORT, salinity, drugs or supplements; animals were fed/held identically apart from room temperature, and no animal received a second developmental treatment. The Q10 values (Table 2, Fig. 4), which are derived across assay temperatures, were correctly excluded.
developmental_timing:
Yes - animals were well before sexual maturity throughout. Tadpoles were collected at Gosner stages 26-29 (Methods, p. 733) and held only 42 days; the species "has a long-lived tadpole stage (up to 8 months)" and tadpoles that hatch in late summer/autumn overwinter (Introduction, p. 732), so the 6-week exposure ended long before metamorphosis, let alone sexual maturity. The treatment did not span development into maturity, so inclusion criterion 3 is satisfied.

The stage coding is right: these are post-hatching free-living larvae, so stage = "postnatal" and all prenatal_* fields correctly left blank; the prenatal/postnatal split is not an issue for this study (the extractor's note about estimating embryo duration and a 1-year maturity age does not affect any field present in this CSV). postnatal_measure_delay = 0 days is also correct - tissue was frozen at the moment of sampling and assayed later, with no post-treatment recovery period.

Two timing caveats feed the findings above: (i) the 0 h samples were taken "immediately before (0 h) temperature change" (p. 733), so those rows precede the developmental manipulation entirely; (ii) the 3 h samples fall inside the 6-hour cooling ramp. Also note the animals were wild-caught rather than laboratory-bred, but the temperature itself was experimentally assigned in constant-temperature rooms, so this is a genuine experimental developmental manipulation and not seasonal field acclimatisation.

On shared controls: sample_depend = 1 and control_multiple_comparisons = "no" on all rows. There is only one treatment level, so no control is reused across doses and "no" is defensible. The real dependency is across measures within a sampling time - "Each individual's tissues were assayed for LDH, CS and CCO activities" (p. 733) - so the CS and CCO rows at a given time (e.g. kris_n_526 and kris_n_537) come from the same 8 + 8 animals, and the five 6-week rows (kris_n_520, 531, 542, 543, 544) all come from that one final cohort. Different sampling times used different animals (176 total), so there is no reuse of a single control group across the time course. sample_depend = 1 appears to capture this adequately, but the analysis should model measure-within-animal correlation for the 6-week rows.

Could not be read directly: the full text (Methods, Fig. 2 caption, Table II) was unobtainable, so I never saw the paper state "mean +/- S.E." vs "+/- S.D.". Verified INDIRECTLY, and the verification is reassuring.

(a) Internal consistency: sd = se * sqrt(n) holds to 4+ significant figures in every cell of all four rows, using n_t1 = 5 and n_t2 = 4 (e.g. CS control 0.1780867 * sqrt(4) = 0.3561733; LDH 15 deg C 25.160008 * sqrt(5) = 56.25949; LDH 30 deg C 18.451459 * sqrt(5) = 41.25872). So the extractor digitised an error bar, treated it as S.E.M., and converted. There is no row where sd == se, i.e. no un-converted SEM.

(b) The conversion is almost certainly in the right direction, because the resulting SDs reproduce the paper's reported significance pattern and the un-converted bars do not. With the sheet's SDs, the only significant contrast is CS at 30 deg C (Welch t = 4.96) while CS at 15 deg C (t = 2.25), LDH at 15 deg C (t = 2.20) and LDH at 30 deg C (t = 2.09) are all non-significant -- exactly the abstract's pattern ("significantly lower citrate synthase" at 30 deg C only; "similar" at 15 deg C; LDH "did not change" at 30 deg C). Had the plotted bars actually been S.D. (so that the true SDs were the smaller se values), CS at 15 deg C would give t = 4.7 and both LDH contrasts t ~ 4.4-4.9, i.e. all four contrasts significant, flatly contradicting the published abstract.

Conclusion: no se-as-sd error, and no evidence the bars were misread as SEM when they were SD. This should still be spot-checked against the Fig. 2 caption once the PDF is obtained, since the check above is conditional on n_t1 = 5 / n_t2 = 4 being right.

The alternative in the paper is Table 5, which reports each group at its own acclimation temperature. Whichever is used should be stated explicitly, and the sheet's stated level (12 C) is not in fact what the extracted numbers correspond to (finding 1). paper_identity: PDF is Stier A, Monaghan P, Metcalfe NB (2022) "Experimental demonstration of prenatal programming of mitochondrial aerobic metabolism lasting until adulthood", Proc. R. Soc. B 289: 20212679 (doi:10.1098/rspb.2021.2679). This matches the sheet metadata (author Stier, year 2022, class Aves, Japanese quail). One trivial error: the sheet spells the genus "Cortunix"; the paper uses Coturnix japonica (p.2, Methods 2a).
error_statistic_reported: SEM. Figure 1 legend (p.4) states explicitly: "means are presented +/- s.e."; the only other error statistics in the paper are 95% CIs on the standardised estimates in Figure 2 and on the repeatability estimates in Figure 3, neither of which was extracted. The sheet handles this correctly: se_* columns hold the digitised SEM and sd_* = se_* * sqrt(n) exactly for all 48 cells (verified numerically), so there is no un-converted-SEM problem in this study.
stated_sample_sizes: The paper states (p.4): "the final dataset includes n = 136 mitochondrial (measurements from n = 76 individuals (L = 20, M = 20, H = 16 and U = 20)). A few (n = 8) ETS values being non-biological (ETS < ROUTINE) were removed". The sheet matches these individual counts: n_t1 = 16 for all 38.4 C (high) rows, n_t1 = 20 for all 37.7 C (medium) rows, n_t2 = 20 for the control rows - correct for ROUTINE, OXPHOS, LEAK and OxCE. For the two ETS-dependent measures (ETS, FCR_R/ETS) the extractor used 14 (high) and 18 (medium/control), assuming the 8 removed ETS values were spread 2 per treatment group; the paper does not say where they came from, and the extractor note documents this assumption, so I accept it. Two caveats worth recording but not, in my view, extraction errors: (i) 136 measurements out of a possible 152 (76 birds x 2 ages) means roughly 16 age-specific measurements are missing, so the true per-age-per-group n is somewhat below 20/20/16 - the paper gives no breakdown, so the stated group sizes are the best available; (ii) the 2-per-group ETS deduction was applied at BOTH ages, which if the 8 removals were spread over both ages makes the ETS/FCR n's about 1 too low per cell (conservative, since it slightly inflates the back-calculated SD).
temperature_treatments: Four prenatal incubation regimes (Methods 2a, p.2): high (H) = 38.4 C constant, medium (M) = 37.7 C constant, low (L) = 37.0 C constant, and unstable (U) = 37.7 C with five 30-min incubation recesses per day giving a 37.0 C daily average. The sheet extracts two contrasts - H vs L (t1 = 38.4, t2 = 37, dose 1.4) and M vs L (t1 = 37.7, t2 = 37, dose 0.7) - and correctly leaves the U group out as a separate treatment, which is right because U is a temperature-stability manipulation rather than a clean mean-temperature contrast. t1 always correctly identifies the treatment group and the t1 means are all correct. The reference assignment (L = 37.0 C as control) follows the paper's own framing (effects are described throughout as relative to the low-temperature group, and L is described as U's "matched control for developmental speed", p.2); note, though, that 37.0 C is at the cold end for artificial incubation of Japanese quail and M (37.7 C) is closest to the standard optimum, so L is arguably a cold treatment rather than a neutral control - a defensible but reviewable choice. The serious problem is execution, not assignment: in Fig 1a and 1b the control CELL was actually read off the unstable (U) series, not the low series (see finding 1), which for the four medium rows reduces the nominal 0.7 C contrast to a 37.7-vs-37.7 stability contrast.
multiple_stressors: Temperature is not crossed with any second developmental manipulation. The only additional factor in the design is temperature STABILITY (the U group), which is a fourth level of the same prenatal treatment rather than a crossed factor, and sex, which was fitted as a covariate (a sex effect on OxCE is reported on p.5); the extracted rows pool both sexes ("both"), matching the plotted group means. No drugs, supplements, diet, UV, hypoxia or CORT manipulation; all birds received identical post-hatching husbandry (21 C rooms, common food, brooder heat removed at day 15, Methods 2a). The respirometry assay temperature was 40.0 C for every sample (Methods 2c, p.3), so there is no acute-test-temperature factor. However, eight rows do in effect draw on a non-baseline level of the stability factor: merged_1/2/7/8/13/14/19/20 use the unstable (U) group as their control (finding 1), which makes those comparisons confounded with the recess/instability manipulation and, for the four medium rows, removes the temperature difference entirely. The 8-OHdG oxidative-damage data were not extracted, correctly - Figure 2 reports only standardised regression slopes, not treatment-group means.
developmental_timing: Yes, the manipulation was entirely pre-hatching and well before sexual maturity. Eggs were incubated at the assigned constant temperature from the start of incubation to hatching (Methods 2a, p.2); the sheet codes stage = "prenatal", prenatal_trt_start = 0, prenatal_trt_end = 16.5, prenatal_dur = 16.5 days, total_trt_duration = 16.5 days with postnatal duration blank, which is consistent with the paper (the exact incubation length is not given in this paper, so the extractor's ~16.5 d estimate from the literature is reasonable for Coturnix japonica) and treatment ended at hatching (Day 0). Quail reach sexual maturity at ca 50 days (p.2), so the manipulation is unambiguously pre-maturity and criterion 1 and the "no treatment spanning into sexual maturity" exclusion are both satisfied. The prenatal/postnatal stage coding is correct. Measurement timing is Day 20 (peak growth) and Day 60 (early adulthood, i.e. after maturity) post-hatch, correctly entered in prenatal_measure_delay as 20 and 60 days except for the two LEAK rows in finding 2; measuring after maturity is not an inclusion problem because the manipulation itself was prenatal.

paper_identity: PDF is Wen B., Jin S.-R., Chen Z.-Z., Gao J.-Z., Wang L., Liu Y., Liu H.-P. (2017) "Plasticity of energy reserves and metabolic performance of discus fish (Symphysodon aequifasciatus) exposed to low-temperature stress", Aquaculture 481: 169-176 (doi 10.1016/j.aquaculture.2017.09.002). This matches the sheet metadata exactly: author Wen, year 2017, genus/species Symphysodon aequifasciatus, class Actinopterygii. "Blue discus fish" is an acceptable common name for S. aequifasciatus. Tissues in the sheet (lateral/skeletal muscle for ETS; liver for ALP/LDH/ALT/AST) match the paper (CEA and ETS measured in muscle, Methods 2.2, p.170; metabolic enzymes measured in liver, Methods 2.4, p.171; Fig. 2 caption "muscle tissue", Fig. 4 caption "liver tissue").
error_statistic_reported: The paper never states what its error bars or "±" values represent. Fig. 2 caption (p.173) and Fig. 4 caption (p.174) describe only the significance lettering; Fig. 3 caption (p.174) says nothing about error; Table 2 (p.175) gives values such as "IBW 9.23 ± 2.01" with no definition; Methods 2.5 (p.171) describes the ANOVA/Bonferroni/Tukey analyses but no dispersion statistic. So criterion 2 ("a reported error statistic") is not satisfied by the paper text itself. The extractor's note records that the authors were contacted and confirmed the bars are standard deviations, which resolves it. This is corroborated internally: Methods 2.1 (p.170) reports "initial body weight 9.24 ± 1.63 g" for the 270 fish, which can only be an among-individual SD, and Table 2's IBW (9.23 ± 2.01, 9.42 ± 1.60, 9.08 ± 1.31) is of the same magnitude. The sheet is coded consistently with SD: sd_* holds the digitised bar length and se_* = sd_*/sqrt(3) on all 40 group cells (verified to <1% on every row), so there is no un-converted-SEM problem here. Note only that if the author confirmation were ever withdrawn, every SD in this study would be a factor of sqrt(3) = 1.73 too small.
stated_sample_sizes: Methods 2.1 (p.170): 270 juveniles into 27 aquaria of 10 fish, 9 aquaria per temperature group; "On days 0, 14 and 28, 30 individuals were randomly sampled from three aquaria of each treatment... The liver and part of the lateral muscle tissues of ten fish were pooled for each biological replicate". That gives 3 pooled biological replicates per temperature x time cell, which is what the sheet records (n_t1 = n_t2 = 3 on all 20 rows). Confirmed independently by Table 1 (p.172): the two-way ANOVA has Temp df = 2, Time df = 2, Temp x time df = 4, consistent with 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 observations (error df = 18). n = 3 is therefore correct, with the caveat that each replicate is a pool of 10 fish (pseudoreplication at the individual level, correctly handled as n = 3). The only other n in the paper is the respirometry n = 3 individual fish (Methods 2.1 and 2.3), which relates to Fig. 3 (OCR) and was not extracted. No n_t1/n_t2 mismatch found.
temperature_treatments: Three experimentally assigned rearing temperatures: 28 C (control), 24 C and 20 C, reached by lowering 1 C/day from 28 C and then held for 28 days (Methods 2.1, p.170). The paper is explicit about the reference group: "The water temperature in the third group was maintained at 28 C to serve as the control treatment", and 28-29 C is the species' optimum (Pirhonen et al. 2014, cited p.170). The sheet assigns t2 = 28 (control) and t1 = 20 or 24 (treatment) on all 20 rows, with dose = -8 and -4 C in celsius - correct and correctly signed. Each of the five measures contributes 4 rows: (20 vs 28) and (24 vs 28) at day 14, and the same pair at day 28. Temperatures, control assignment and dose are all right; no wrong-group or reversed-comparison problem was found.
multiple_stressors: No second experimental stressor. The design is temperature-only, crossed with exposure time (0, 14, 28 d) as a repeated sampling factor, not with UV, hypoxia, diet, CORT, salinity or acute assay temperature (Methods 2.1, p.170; Table 1, p.172, tests only Temp, Time and Temp x time). Feeding was identical across groups ("beef heart hamburger" at 5% wet mass during the 30-day pre-trial acclimation, Methods 2.1); no drug or supplement was given. Exposure time is the only other factor, and all sheet rows come from days 14 and 28, both legitimate levels. One measurement-temperature caveat worth recording but not a violation: the ETS assay itself was run at a single fixed 20 C for all groups (Methods 2.2, p.170: "The reaction was started by adding 100 uL 8 mM p-iodonitrotetrazolium to proceed at 20 C for 10 min"), so ETS rows are common-garden assays and not confounded by assay temperature. Respirometry (Fig. 3, not extracted) was instead run at each group's own holding temperature (Methods 2.3, p.171: "The magnetic stirrer was set at the same temperature at which the fish were being maintained"), i.e. OCR would have been confounded with acute test temperature - another reason its exclusion is appropriate. Criterion 3 is met: no animal received a second developmental manipulation, and this is an experimentally assigned laboratory temperature, not seasonal/field acclimatisation.
developmental_timing:
Yes, animals were pre-sexual-maturity throughout. The paper calls them "juvenile discus fish" with initial body weight 9.24 ± 1.63 g (Methods 2.1, p.170) and frames the work as guidance for "the juvenile S. aequifasciatus" (Abstract, p.169; Discussion, p.175). The paper itself gives no age, so the sheet's postnatal_trt_start = 255 days is the extractor's documented estimate (7.5 months median age at 12-18 month maturity, cross-checked against Satora et al. 2022, plus the paper's 30-day pre-trial acclimation). Treatment runs to day 268 or 282 (~9-9.4 months), still below the 12-18 month maturity window, so criterion 1 is met and criterion 3's "spanning development into sexual maturity" exclusion does not bite. Note the estimate is soft: it rests on body mass, not on any age reported by the authors, and if these fish were older than ~11 months the exposure would approach maturity - worth carrying as an uncertainty flag rather than a correction.

The stage coding is right: stage = "postnatal", all prenatal fields (prenatal_trt_start/end, prenatal_dur, prenatal_unit, prenatal_measure_delay) left blank, and postnatal_measure_delay = 0 because fish were killed and sampled at the day-14/day-28 sampling points with no recovery interval (Methods 2.1, p.170). sex = "both" is an assumption the paper does not state (no sexing is reported), but is reasonable for randomly allocated juveniles and is not a reportable error. The one timing inaccuracy is the treatment-duration bookkeeping described in the findings: the 1 C/day ramp (8 days for the 20 C group, 4 days for the 24 C group) is not included in dur_trt_postnatal, and six day-14 rows carry total_trt_duration = 28 instead of 14.

paper_identity: The PDF is Akhtar MS, Pal AK, Sahu NP, Ciji A, Mahanta PC (2013) "Thermal tolerance, oxygen consumption and haemato-biochemical variables of Tor putitora juveniles acclimated to five temperatures", Fish Physiology and Biochemistry 39:1387-1398, DOI 10.1007/s10695-013-9793-7. This matches the sheet metadata exactly: author Akhtar, year 2013, Tor putitora / golden mahseer, class Actinopterygii. Citation "Akhtar_et_al_2013" is correct.
error_statistic_reported: SEM. Table 2 footnote (p. 1392): "Mean values bearing different superscripts (a, b, c and d) under each column vary significantly (P < 0.05). Data expressed as mean +/- SE, n = 6". Table 3 footnote (p. 1393): identical wording, "mean +/- SE, n = 6". Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 captions also state "Data expressed as mean +/- SE", and the Methods report body weight as "13.62 +/- 2.15 g, average weight +/- SE" (p. 1388). The sheet handles this correctly: se_t1/se_t2 hold the printed table values verbatim and sd_t1/sd_t2 = se * sqrt(6). I checked all 72 mean/SE pairs programmatically; every SD equals se*sqrt(n) to within rounding, so there is no un-converted SEM anywhere in this study. CI95 columns are appropriately empty (the paper reports no CIs).
stated_sample_sizes: n = 6 per temperature group for all enzyme assays, and this matches n_t1 = n_t2 = 6 in all 36 rows. Methods, Enzyme assays, p. 1390: "At the end of the acclimation trial, six fish from each acclimation temperature group were killed and different tissues like liver, gill, kidney and brain were dissected out"; both table footnotes repeat "n = 6". Note two design caveats that do not contradict the sheet: (i) fish were stocked in triplicate tanks per temperature (Methods p. 1389, "randomly distributed in five acclimation temperature groups in triplicates"), so n = 6 is fish, not tanks; (ii) the same 6 fish per temperature supplied liver, gill and kidney and all three enzymes, so the 9 rows within a given temperature share animals - which the sheet's sample_depend (1 = 32 C, 2 = 29 C, 3 = 26 C, 4 = 23 C) does capture. Other n values in the paper (n = 20 for CTmax/LTmax and oxygen consumption, Fig. 1a-b) belong to measures that were not extracted.
temperature_treatments: Five acclimation temperatures, 20, 23, 26, 29 and 32 +/- 0.5 C (Abstract p. 1387; Methods p. 1389). The biologically appropriate control is 20 C: it is the paper's first/reference group ("The first group was maintained at temperature of 20 C"), it equals the 10-day pre-trial acclimatisation temperature, it is closest to the source pond temperature of 19.5 C, and the species "thrives well in the temperature range of 20-25 C" (Introduction p. 1387). The sheet assigns t2 = 20 for every row and t1 = 32, 29, 26 or 23, i.e. treatment = elevated, control = 20 C, which is correct; `dose` (12, 9, 6, 3) and units.1 = celsius are right. The temperatures were experimentally assigned at random ("randomly distributed in five acclimation temperature groups in triplicates following a completely randomized design") and reached by ramping 1 C/day, then held 30 days - so despite the paper's use of the word "acclimation", this is an experimental developmental temperature manipulation, not field/seasonal acclimatisation, and the exclusion criterion on seasonal acclimatisation does not bite.
multiple_stressors: No second experimental factor is crossed with temperature for any extracted row. Design is a one-way, five-level temperature experiment (Methods p. 1389); all enzyme assays were run at a common assay temperature of 37 C for every group (footnotes to Tables 2 and 3), so there is no acute-assay-temperature crossing in these rows. Three things to note but none disqualifies a row: (i) all fish, before group assignment, received a routine prophylactic 1% NaCl 5-min bath and a 5 ppm KMnO4 dip during transfer (p. 1388-1389) - applied uniformly pre-randomisation, so not a second developmental manipulation; (ii) water quality co-varied with temperature as a consequence of the treatment (Table 1, p. 1391: dissolved oxygen fell 6.97 to 5.70 mg/L, pH fell 8.10 to 6.57, ammonia-N rose 0.01 to 0.23 mg/L from 20 to 32 C), which is a confound intrinsic to warming rather than an assigned factor; (iii) the CTmax/LTmax and oxygen-consumption measurements were made at each group's own temperature, but those rows were not extracted. All 36 sheet rows come from the single baseline design, so criterion 4 is satisfied.
developmental_timing: Animals were pre-sexual-maturity, so criterion 1 is met, and the stage coding is right. The paper studies "Juveniles of T. putitora (13.62 +/- 2.15 g)" collected from ponds (p. 1388), grown to 15.81 g by the end of the 30-day trial; Tor putitora does not mature until roughly 4+ years, so 14 g fish are well short of maturity and the 30-day treatment cannot span into maturity. stage = "postnatal" with all prenatal columns empty is correct for an externally developing fish exposed post-hatch; postnatal_measure_delay = 0 is correct because tissues were taken at the end of the acclimation trial (p. 1390). The one soft spot is the imputed age: the paper gives no age at all ("juveniles" only), and the extractor derived post_natal_trt_start = 843.25 d (= 821.25 + 10 d acclimatisation + 12 d ramp) by halving a 4.5-year median adult age. For 13.6 g mahseer this is plausibly a substantial over-estimate of true age, and the 12-day ramp was applied uniformly even though the ramp lasted only 3, 6, 9 and 12 days for the 23, 26, 29 and 32 C groups respectively. The assumption is documented in the extractor note and applied consistently, so I have not raised it as a finding, but any age- or timing-based moderator for this study should be treated as an imputation, not a paper-stated value.

paper_identity: PDF is: Ale A, Bacchetta C, Rossi AS, Scarabotti PA, Cazenave J (2021) "Low temperature stress in a cultured fish (Piaractus mesopotamicus) fed with Pyropia columbina red seaweed-supplemented diet." Fish Physiology and Biochemistry 47:829-839, doi 10.1007/s10695-021-00944-7. This matches the sheet metadata (author Ale, year 2021, Piaractus mesopotamicus, pacu, Actinopterygii). No identity mismatch.
error_statistic_reported: The paper reports SE. Methods, "Statistical analyses", p. 832 (PDF p. 4): "All results were reported as mean +/- standard error (SE)." The Table 2, 3 and 4 captions repeat "Values are expressed as means +/- SE" / are described in the same terms. The only SD in the paper is in Table 1 (diet chemical composition, "expressed as mean +/- SD (n = 3)"), which is not used by the sheet. The sheet handled this correctly in form: se_t1/se_t2 reproduce the paper's +/- values exactly on all 15 rows and sd_* = se_* x sqrt(n) everywhere (e.g. merged_112 sd_t2 = 24.72 x 3 = 74.16; merged_124 sd_t2 = 0.007 x sqrt(6) = 0.017146). No row has sd == se, so there is no un-converted SEM. The residual problem is the n used in that conversion, not the conversion itself.
stated_sample_sizes:
The paper states three different n's for three different sets of measures. Exposure: "fish fed with CD or RD (n = 18 per diet) to control (24 +/- 0.1 C) or cold temperature (14 +/- 0.1 C) in 10-L aquaria (n = 3 per aquarium, in triplicate)" (p. 831) - 9 fish per diet x temperature cell. Haematology (Table 2) and plasma metabolites (Table 3): n = 9. Tissue energy reserves: n = 6. Oxidative stress, which is all the sheet uses: "Enzyme extracts from the liver, intestine, gills, and muscle of fish (n = 6)" and "lipid peroxidation levels (n = 6)" (p. 832).

Against the sheet: the three TBARS rows (merged_114, 119, 124) use n = 6, which matches the stated per-cell n. The twelve enzyme rows (merged_110-113, 115-118, 120-123) use n = 9, which does not - 9 is the exposure/haematology n, not the Table 4 n. Additionally, because 12 of the 15 rows were taken from the diet-pooled temperature marginal columns rather than a single diet x temperature cell, the correct n for those rows is 12 (6 CD + 6 RD), so no row that uses a marginal mean has the right n: the enzyme ones are too low (9 vs 12) and the TBARS ones lower still (6 vs 12). Only merged_110 and merged_113 are genuine single-cell (CD) means, and for those the correct n is 6 rather than the recorded 9.
temperature_treatments: Two temperatures, 14 +/- 0.1 C (cold shock) and 24 +/- 0.1 C (control), applied for 24 h in artificial climate chambers (Methods, p. 831). 24 C is unambiguously the control/reference: fish were acclimated and held at 24 +/- 1 C beforehand, the paper calls 24 C the "control temperature" (Abstract, p. 829; Methods, p. 831), and "Optimal range for pacu culture is 20-28 C" (p. 830) while 14 C is chosen as a sub-optimal stressor relative to a ~7-7.5 C lethal limit. The sheet assigns t1 = 14 (treatment) and t2 = 24 (control) with dose = -10 C on all 15 rows, which is correct and consistently oriented: every mean_t1 is the paper's 14 C value and every mean_t2 the 24 C value (verified cell by cell against Table 4). No treatment/control inversion anywhere.
multiple_stressors:
Yes - the design is a fully crossed 2 x 2 of temperature (24 vs 14 C) and DIET (control diet CD vs Pyropia columbina red-seaweed-supplemented diet RD), analysed by two-way ANOVA (p. 832). Every animal received one of the two diets for 60 days before the thermal exposure; CD is the baseline level.

Rows drawn from non-baseline levels of that second factor: none is purely RD, but twelve of fifteen rows are diet-POOLED temperature marginal means and therefore half RD animals - merged_111 (liver CAT), merged_112 (liver GST), merged_114 (liver TBARS), merged_116-119 (gill CAT, GST, GR, TBARS) and merged_120-124 (muscle SOD, CAT, GST, GR, TBARS). Only merged_110 (liver SOD) and merged_113 (liver GR) use the CD-only "Simple main effects" cells, i.e. the baseline diet. merged_115 (gill SOD) is nominally labelled CD in the table but comes from the corrupt duplicated block and is really intestine GST. The paper publishes CD-only cell means for only three parameters in Table 4 (liver SOD, liver GR, intestine GST), the three with a significant temperature x diet interaction, so baseline-only extraction is simply not possible for the remaining parameters without author contact. The seaweed supplement is also a bioactive additive ("P. columbina has bioactive compounds with antioxidant properties (Cian et al. 2014)", p. 830) given alongside the stressor, which touches the exclusion for supplement co-treatment. There is no second temperature factor: assays were run on frozen tissue, not at multiple acute test temperatures. Nothing else (UV, hypoxia, salinity, CORT) is manipulated.
developmental_timing:
Animals were pre-sexual-maturity, but only just, and the "developmental" framing is strained. Fish were purchased as juveniles at 7.0 +/- 0.5 cm standard length and 12.2 +/- 2.5 g (p. 831), the paper consistently calls them "juvenile Piaractus mesopotamicus" (Abstract; Discussion p. 833), and pacu mature at roughly two years (the extractor's external reference, Gelman et al. 2004), so sexual maturity was not reached during the study and the treatment does not span into maturity. The paper itself gives no ages, so the ages in the sheet are imputed.

The stage coding "postnatal" is right for a fish with no maternal/prenatal manipulation - all prenatal fields are correctly blank. The duration coding is also faithful to the paper: post_natal_trt_start = 439, postnatal_trt_end = 440, dur_trt_postnatal = 1 day, total_trt_duration = 1 day, postnatal_measure_delay = 0 days, matching a 24-h exposure with sampling immediately afterwards ("After 24 h, animals were anesthetized", p. 831). Two caveats: (1) the absolute age 439 days conflicts with the extractor's own derivation in the note (285 + 14 + 60 = 359), an 80-day internal inconsistency; (2) substantively, a single 24-h cold shock applied to a ~1-year-old juvenile after a 60-day feeding trial is an acute thermal challenge rather than a developmental temperature regime - the authors describe it as "cold shock" in the title, keywords and throughout - so whether it satisfies criterion 1 is a judgement the review team should make explicitly rather than by default.
coverage:
All 15 rows trace to Table 4 (p. 835, PDF page 7), "Antioxidant enzyme activities and TBARS levels in the liver, intestine, gills, and muscle". The PDF is the extractor's working copy with yellow highlights, so I could confirm cell-by-cell which numbers were taken. Every se_t1/se_t2 in the sheet reproduces the paper's "± SE" value exactly, and sd = se x sqrt(n) was applied consistently with the n the extractor entered, so the arithmetic is clean; the problems are which cell and which n.

Mapping (t1 = 14 C, t2 = 24 C): merged_110 liver SOD = Table 4 "Simple main effects CD" row (14.81+/-1.96, 44.57+/-6.37); merged_113 liver GR = "Simple main effects CD" row (33.98+/-5.08, 67.36+/-11.14). These two are genuine control-diet cell means. merged_111 liver CAT, merged_112 liver GST, merged_114 liver TBARS, merged_116-119 gill CAT/GST/GR/TBARS, merged_120-124 muscle SOD/CAT/GST/GR/TBARS all come from the diet-POOLED "Temperature 24 C / 14 C" marginal columns (highlighted as such). merged_115 comes from the corrupt "Gills SOD / Mann-Whitney CD" row (see finding).

Autoflags: all three are FALSE ALARMS as stated. merged_114 sd_t1 == sd_t2 (0.0244949) simply reflects Table 4 liver TBARS reporting 0.18 +/- 0.01 and 0.27 +/- 0.01, i.e. identical SEs with identical n. merged_119 sd_t1 == sd_t2 (0.220454) reflects gill TBARS 0.94 +/- 0.09 and 1.03 +/- 0.09, again identical SEs. merged_124 mean_t1 == mean_t2 == 0.085 is exactly what Table 4 prints for muscle TBARS (0.085 +/- 0.007 at 24 C, 0.085 +/- 0.006 at 14 C) - a true null, not a copy error. The paper states (p. 5, "Experimental setup", and repeated in the Fig. 3 caption): "two pooled samples (one from each tank) were taken at each temperature point, comprising of 20 live individuals each." So n = 2 pooled samples per temperature, each pool = 20 larvae. The sheet's n_t1 = n_t2 = 2 matches what the paper reports, and the extractor note records the pooling correctly.

Caveat worth knowing downstream (not scored as a separate finding): the two "replicates" are the two rearing tanks (Fig. 1, p. 4), and both tanks sat in a single shared temperature-controlled water bath driven by one circulator, so n = 2 is tank-level pseudo-replication of a single thermal unit, and the units of replication are pools of 20 larvae rather than individuals. temperature_treatments:
There is no set of independently reared temperature groups. Larvae (12 days post-hatch, ~4.4-5 mm) were held at 18 C for 24 h and then subjected to a single continuous ramp of +1 C per hour from 18 C to the cumulative CTmax of 30 C (p. 5). Pooled samples were taken at 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28 and 30 C from the same two tanks as the ramp progressed.

The paper explicitly designates 18 C as the control/reference: the Fig. 3 caption calls it "the control temperature (18 C)"; Methods p. 6 expresses protein carbonylation "taking the control temperature 18 C as reference"; Results p. 7 compares each level "when compared to control conditions (18 C)"; and p. 9 refers to "larvae subjected to 18 C (controls)". The sheet's t1 = 18 + 6 = 24 C is wrong for these rows. Every extracted treatment mean and SD comes from the 30 C bar (see finding 1), so t1 should be 30 and dose should be 12 C, not 6 C. The extractor note explains the 24: "used the average temperature exposure for 24 hours", i.e. the midpoint of an 18-30 C ramp. That reasoning is defensible in principle, but it collides with the fact that 24 C is itself a real, separately plotted sampling level with materially different values, and it understates the actual thermal dose of the extracted samples by half.

No second experimental manipulation is crossed with temperature. Salinity (25 per mille), oxygen (95-100%) and feeding (rotifers and Artemia every 6 h) were held constant, and no drug, supplement, UV, hypoxia or diet factor was applied (pp. 4-5). So criterion 4 (non-baseline level of a second factor) is not violated in the usual sense, and no sheet row comes from a non-baseline level of another treatment.

The complication is that temperature here IS the acute assay variable rather than a developmental rearing treatment: the design is a CTmax determination by dynamic ramping at 1 C/h, so each "temperature group" is a time point along one acute heat challenge. The specific level the sheet extracted (30 C) is the cumulative CTmax itself, defined as the temperature at which 100% of larvae were lethargic, with 80% relative mortality (Results p. 7, Fig. 2). That makes the extracted treatment group survivors of a near-lethal acute challenge (see findings 3 and 4).
developmental_timing:
Yes, animals were unambiguously pre-sexual-maturity. Larvae were obtained at 11 days post-hatch and were 12 days post-hatch when the experiment ran (p. 4-5); the larval phase alone lasts ~50 days at 17-18 C (Table 1, p. 3), and sexual maturity in S. aurata is years away. At 12 dph the larvae had pectoral fins, eye pigmentation, primary swim bladder inflation and ~100% yolk-sac reabsorption.

The prenatal/postnatal coding in the sheet is right: stage = "postnatal", post-hatch treatment window recorded in the postnatal columns, all prenatal fields blank, postnatal_measure_delay = 0 days. Exposure did not span into sexual maturity, so criterion 3 is not violated on that ground.

The coded duration is the weak point: post_natal_trt_start = 12, postnatal_trt_end = 13, dur = 1 day. At 1 C/h, 30 C is reached ~12 h after the ramp starts (and 24 C at ~6 h), so the actual exposure is roughly half a day of continuously rising temperature, not a day at a fixed temperature. The extractor note's "temp was increased by 1C per hour for 24 hours" is a misreading; the 24 h in the paper is the pre-experiment acclimation at 18 C. More fundamentally, a ~12 h ramp is an acute thermal-tolerance challenge rather than a developmental temperature manipulation (finding 3).

error_statistic_reported:
The paper reports SD explicitly. Fig. 1 caption (p. 1009): "Error bars represent mean ± SD (n = 8)". Fig. 2 caption (p. 1010): "Error bars represent mean ± SD (n = 8)". No SEM or CI is reported anywhere.

The sheet handled this correctly. I verified numerically that the sd_* columns equal the plotted error-bar half-lengths (not 2.83x them), so the digitised SD went into sd_* and se_* was back-computed as sd/sqrt(8). Examples: Fig. 2a larvae 10 °C cap measured at 0.97/1.09 vs sd_t2 = 1.018 (se_t2 = 0.360 would be far too short); Fig. 1b 1-month 16 °C cap measured at 159.5 vs sd_t1 = 162.8 (se_t1 = 57.5 would not fit); Fig. 2b 1-month 14 °C cap measured at 0.00352 vs sd_t1 = 0.00349. There is no se-as-sd problem in this study. The only error-statistic defect is the two copy-pasted se_t1 cells in merged_294/295 (finding 2).
stated_sample_sizes:
n = 8 per developmental stage per temperature, stated three independent times: (1) p. 1007, "Eight individuals of each stage were placed in each of four 5-L aquaria"; (2) p. 1007, "Eight bottles containing animals were incubated at each of 10, 12, 14 and 16 °C"; (3) both figure captions, "(n = 8)", and the Table 1 footnote (p. 1010), "n = 8 per each experimental temperature, i.e. 10, 12, 14, 16 °C".

The sheet records n_t1 = 8 and n_t2 = 8 on all 27 rows. This matches the paper exactly - no n discrepancy.

Caveat (not an extraction error, the sheet faithfully records what the paper states): each temperature was a single 5-L aquarium, so the 8 individuals per cell are tank-mates and temperature is unreplicated at the tank level. CAT/GR were assayed in duplicate and ETS in triplicate, but those are technical replicates and do not change n.
temperature_treatments:
Four levels: 10 °C (control), 12, 14 and 16 °C. Control is unambiguous - p. 1007: "Eight individuals of each stage were placed in each of four 5-L aquaria with continuously aerated water at 10 °C. One, the control, was maintained at a constant 10 °C." 10 °C also matches the hatchery spring-water rearing temperature (10.0 ± 0.5 °C, raised to 11.0 ± 0.5 °C after hatch, p. 1007), so it is the biologically appropriate reference.

The sheet assigns this correctly on all 27 rows: t1 = 16, 14 or 12 (treatment) and t2 = 10 (control), with mean_t1/sd_t1/n_t1 from the warm group and mean_t2/sd_t2/n_t2 from the 10 °C bar. The dose column (6, 4, 2 °C with units.1 = celsius) is the correct t1 - t2 increment. No t1/t2 inversion and no wrong-temperature row found.
multiple_stressors:
Temperature is not crossed with any external second manipulation - no UV, hypoxia, diet, CORT, salinity or drug treatment. Fish were unfed during the 96 h exposure period apart from normal hatchery feeding, and survival was 100 % at all temperatures (p. 1007). Developmental stage (eyed eggs / yolk-sac larvae / 1-month / 3-month juveniles) is the second factor in the paper's two-way ANOVA, but that is the review's own stage covariate rather than a co-stressor, and the sheet correctly keeps each stage's 10 °C group as its own control.

There IS, however, a crossed ACUTE ASSAY TEMPERATURE for the ETS measure, which the review's criterion 4 names explicitly. Per p. 1008 the ETS reaction was "incubated for 25 min at 10, 12, 14 or 16 °C", i.e. at each group's own exposure temperature, so no baseline-assay-temperature level exists for these rows. All 9 ETS rows (merged_299-307) therefore come from a non-baseline level of that second factor - this is finding 1. The CAT and GR assays were run at a common 25 °C for every group (p. 1008), so the 18 antioxidant rows are clean on this point.
developmental_timing:
Yes, all extracted animals were far from sexual maturity. Marble trout mature at several years of age (the paper's broodstock were 11 years old, p. 1007); the extracted rows are yolk-sac larvae and juveniles of 1 and 3 months, with body masses of 72-110 mg, 65-216 mg and 330-863 mg respectively (p. 1007). Criterion 1 (manipulation before sexual maturity) and criterion 3 (no spanning of development into sexual maturity) are both satisfied.

Prenatal/postnatal coding is correct: stage = "postnatal" on all 27 rows, and every row has the prenatal_* columns blank. All three extracted stages are post-hatch ("A total of 7600 eyed eggs started to hatch at 470 degree-days. The larvae (7100) were reared in a trough for 21 days", p. 1007), and the one pre-hatch stage - eyed eggs - was deliberately left out (extractor note: "we used larvae as they have hatched"). postnatal_measure_delay = 0 days is also right: tissue was sampled immediately after the 96 h exposure and the respirometry run (p. 1008, animals "frozen in liquid nitrogen" straight after incubation).

Two timing caveats: (a) the ages 21/30/90 days used for post_natal_trt_start are the extractor's reasonable reading of "larvae reared in a trough for 21 days" and "juveniles aged 1 month and 3 months" - the paper never gives exact days post-hatch, so these are approximations rather than errors; (b) the exposure itself is a short 96 h acute thermal challenge at a fixed stage, not a chronic developmental rearing-temperature manipulation - in scope under criterion 1, but the duration coding understates it (finding 3) and it may deserve a chronic-vs-acute moderator.

temperature_treatments:
Embryonic temperature (TE) was manipulated at three levels: 22 degC (cold extreme), 27 degC (near-optimal) and 32 degC (warm extreme), each ±0.5 degC (Methods "Experiment 2/3", p. 1379). The paper is unambiguous that 27 degC is the control: the Abstract calls it "a control TE (27 degC)", the Results (p. 1371) call it "near-optimal thermal conditions (27 degC)" and refer throughout to "the 27 degC TE controls", and all Bonferroni comparisons in Fig. 2A are "a significant difference from the 27 degC TE group".

The sheet assigns this correctly: t2 = 27 on all 10 rows (control), t1 = 22 on the five odd rows and t1 = 32 on the five even rows, with dose = -5 and +5 degC respectively. Tissue, measure identity and units are also correctly matched per row. The only temperature-metadata issue is that the exposure duration is not group-specific (see the low-severity duration finding).
multiple_stressors:
Yes — the design crosses TE with two further factors, but the extracted rows come from the baseline level of both, so there is no inclusion-criterion-4 violation.

(1) Adult acclimation temperature (TA): at 3 months of age fish from each TE group were acclimated to either 27 degC or 32 degC for 30 days (Methods, p. 1379). 27 degC is the baseline (it equals the common post-hatch rearing temperature).
(2) Assay temperature (Ta): enzymes were assayed at 22, 27, 32 and 36 degC. 27 degC is the baseline.

Fig. 2A, the source of all 10 rows, is the TA = 27 / Ta = 27 cell. This is established by the Results text on p. 1371 ("adult zebrafish that were raised at a common 27 degC after hatching, as reflected by differences in maximal enzyme activities assayed at 27 degC (Fig. 2A)"), the Fig. 2 caption ("adult zebrafish that were raised at 27 degC after hatching"), and decisively by the Table 2 caption (p. 1373): "Maximal enzyme activities (Vmax ...) of fish acclimated to 27 degC and assayed at 27 degC were regressed to body mass ... that are shown in Fig. 2B" — Fig. 2B is the individual-level scatter of the same data summarised in Fig. 2A. I also cross-checked Fig. 6 (CS): its 27 degC-acclimation points at a 27 degC assay temperature reproduce the Fig. 2A CS bars (~0.24 for both the 27 and 32 degC TE groups).

No rows are drawn from the 32 degC acclimation group or from the 22/32/36 degC assay temperatures, and no drug, diet, hypoxia or UV manipulation exists in this study. Nothing to flag here.
developmental_timing:
Correct and clearly pre-maturity. The temperature manipulation was confined to the embryonic period: embryos were collected at the 1-8 cell stage (within ~1-2.5 h post-fertilisation; Methods p. 1379) and raised at 22, 27 or 32 degC only until hatching, after which "larvae were maintained at a common temperature of 27±0.5 degC". Zebrafish hatch at ~48-72 h post-fertilisation and reach sexual maturity at ~3 months, so the treatment ended roughly three months before maturity — well inside criterion 1, and not a treatment "spanning development into sexual maturity".

The prenatal/postnatal coding is appropriate for an externally developing oviparous fish: the sheet uses the prenatal_* fields (start 1.5 h, end 60 h post-fertilisation) for the pre-hatching exposure and leaves the postnatal_* fields blank, with stage = "prenatal". That maps correctly onto the paper's design.

Two timing values are nevertheless misstated and are reported as low-severity findings: (a) a single 58.5 h duration is used for all three TE groups even though exposure ran to hatching and developmental rate differed 2.33-fold between 22 and 32 degC (~89 h vs ~38 h); (b) prenatal_measure_delay = 90 days, whereas the enzyme samples were taken at the end of a 30-day acclimation that began at 3 months of age, i.e. ~120 days post-fertilisation (Methods p. 1379; Discussion p. 1374 "sampled at 4 months of age").

Note also that the post-maturity 30-day acclimation at 27 or 32 degC is an adult manipulation, not a developmental one, and the rows use only its 27 degC baseline level, so it does not compromise the developmental-timing coding.

The paper states n=76 (26.5 C low), n=78 (27.1 C medium) and n=76 (27.7 C high) in both the Methods (p. 563) and the Fig. 2C legend (p. 566). The follow-up ANCOVA degrees of freedom also imply N = 214 analysed individuals (F1,192 for temperature with 1 df season + 19 df clutch-within-season => 192+21+1 = 214), and the clutch x treatment ANOVA (F38,151) implies roughly the same. So the true per-group assayed n are probably ~71-72 rather than 76/78/76, which would inflate the derived sd_* by about 4%. Since the sheet reproduces exactly what the paper states, I am not raising this as a finding, but it is worth recording if n is used for weighting sensitivity.
temperature_treatments:
Experiment 3 (the only experiment extracted) assigned eggs within each clutch (split-clutch, 21 clutches) to one of three 24 h sinusoidal fluctuating regimes: 26.5+-2 C (low), 27.1+-2 C (medium) or 27.7+-2 C (high), with CTEs of 26.9, 27.5 and 28.0 C respectively (Methods p. 563; Fig. 1C).

There is no designated control group in this design - it is a three-level mean-temperature gradient. The sheet uses the intermediate 27.1 C (medium) group as the reference (t2) for both contrasts: merged_328/330 compare high 27.7 C (t1) against 27.1 C (dose +0.6), and merged_329/331 compare low 26.5 C (t1) against 27.1 C (dose -0.6). Using the intermediate level as the reference is the biologically appropriate choice here, and the signed `dose` column preserves the fact that one contrast is a warming and the other a cooling manipulation - important because the paper's significant effect is that the LOW temperature group had ELEVATED TAC (Fig. 2C asterisk on the low/triangle point; MANOVA F4,76 = 4.23, P = 0.004; ANCOVA slope -2.41 umol l-1 Trolox equiv mg-1 ww per C, P < 0.0001). Downstream analyses must respect the sign of `dose`, otherwise the cooling contrast will be pooled as if it were a warming contrast.

Other temperatures in the paper, not extracted: Experiment 1 constant 29.5 C vs fluctuating 28.7+-3 C; Experiment 2 28.7+-3 C with 12/24/48 h fluctuation periods (all CTE 29.4 C).
multiple_stressors:
No. Experiment 3 crosses mean incubation temperature with nothing else that was manipulated. The only other terms in the design are nesting season (early vs late clutch collection, 10 and 11 clutches) and clutch identity, both of which are blocking/observational variables rather than experimental manipulations, and neither was significant for TAC or damage (Table 2: Season P = 0.125, Season x Treatment P = 0.198). The Fig. 2C means are pooled across season, so no row is drawn from a non-baseline level of a second factor. All groups were incubated in the same vermiculite/hydric conditions (-150 kPa, ~100% humidity) and all hatchlings were subsequently held at 24-26 C, i.e. common-garden post-hatch.

One thing worth recording but not a violation: "Hatchlings from the fluctuation frequency and mean temperature experiments were involved in other projects (Bowden et al., 2014; Carter et al., 2016; A.W.C., unpublished data) and could not be euthanized until these later dates" (Methods p. 564). Carter et al. 2016 (Physiol. Behav. 155, 46-55) is "Turtle hatchlings show behavioral types that are robust to developmental manipulations" - i.e. non-invasive behavioural assays applied to all animals across all thermal groups. This is a shared, non-differential handling protocol, not a second developmental manipulation, no drugs or supplements are mentioned, and it does not cross temperature with another factor. It therefore does not trigger the exclusion criteria, although it does mean the hatchlings had 37-44 days of behavioural testing before sampling.
developmental_timing:
Correct. The manipulation is entirely prenatal/embryonic: eggs were collected within 6 h of laying (Methods p. 563) and the temperature regime was applied for the whole of incubation until pip, so stage = "prenatal" with prenatal_trt_start = 0 and prenatal_trt_end = 70 is the right coding, and postnatal treatment fields are correctly blank. The 70-day incubation duration is an inference (the paper reports incubation period only as a covariate, never as a mean); the note declares the basis (60-80 days from Tucker 1997, median taken), which is reasonable, though note that the 26.5 C group will genuinely have incubated longer than the 27.7 C group.

prenatal_measure_delay = 40.5 days is correct: "Hatchlings were euthanized by an intrapleuroperitoneal injection of pentobarbital sodium solution between ... 37 and 44 days post-pip (mean temperature)" (Methods p. 564), median 40.5. Sampling was therefore ~5-6 weeks post-hatch in hatchling turtles, far short of sexual maturity in Trachemys scripta elegans (several years), so criterion 1 ("before sexual maturity") and the exclusion of treatments spanning into sexual maturity are both satisfied.

Minor, not reported as a finding: sex = "both" is an assumption - the paper never reports hatchling sex, and given temperature-dependent sex determination in this species these below-pivotal CTEs (26.9-28.0 C) would likely have produced predominantly males. "both" is acceptable as unknown/mixed but should not be read as a verified mixed-sex sample.

multiple_stressors:
Temperature is the only developmental manipulation - there is no UV, hypoxia, diet, CORT, salinity or drug/supplement factor crossed with it, and no animal received a second developmental treatment. After hatching both groups went into the same enclosure at a constant 25 C on a 12:12 light-dark cycle with heat lamps and ad libitum water and commercial chicken starter feed (Methods, p. R2316), i.e. a common garden identical for both groups, so the post-hatch measurements at +4 and +8 days are not confounded by a second manipulation.

The one second factor present is an ACUTE ASSAY temperature, and it affects the 8 enzyme-activity rows only: "Assays for COX and citrate synthase (CS) were determined in duplicate at 35 degrees C and 40 degrees C" and assay temperature was entered as the repeated measure in the RM-ANOVA (Methods, p. R2316). Figs 3C/3D and 6C/6D, however, plot only one point per incubation group per age and neither caption says which assay temperature (or whether the two were pooled) - I confirmed at 500 dpi that there is a single series per treatment, not two. So merged_340-343 (liver COX and CS activity) and merged_352-355 (muscle COX and CS activity) come from a figure that collapses this second factor, and it cannot be verified that they are the baseline level. This is reported as a low-severity provenance finding; it does not change any mean, SE or n. The 16 mRNA rows are unaffected (qPCR has no acute assay-temperature factor).
developmental_timing:
Yes - the animals were far from sexual maturity throughout, and the prenatal/postnatal coding is right. The temperature manipulation was applied to eggs from the start of artificial incubation until hatching (normothermic internal piping day 19/20 and hatching day 20/21; hypothermic piping day 22/23 and hatching day 23/24, Methods p. R2316), i.e. entirely prenatal/embryonic, and it stopped at hatching when both groups were moved to a common 25 C brooder. The measured chicks were 4 and 8 days post-hatch - domestic fowl reach sexual maturity at roughly 5 months (the paper's own adult reference birds were 452 days old) - so the treatment neither spanned into sexual maturity nor did measurement occur after it.

Sheet coding is consistent with this: stage = "prenatal", prenatal_trt_start = 0, prenatal_trt_end = 22.5, prenatal_dur = 22.5 days, total_trt_duration = 22.5 days, all postnatal_trt_* blank, and prenatal_measure_delay = 4 or 8 days (postnatal_measure_delay blank, measure_delay_units = days). Two small, documented approximations, neither of which affects an effect size and neither of which I am reporting as a finding: (i) prenatal_trt_start = 0 assumes the eggs entered incubation at laying - the paper only says fertilized eggs were obtained from a local supplier, as the extractor note states; (ii) treatment duration actually differed between groups by design (hatching day 20/21 in the 38 C group vs day 23/24 in the 35 C group), so a single 22.5-day value is a compromise for two different durations - the midpoint of 20.5 and 23.5 days is 22.0 rather than 22.5, a 0.5-day rounding. sex = "both" is an assumption; the paper never reports the sex of the chicks, so it cannot be verified either way.
